title: Fatimah al-Zahra
hookLine: his youngest daughter, of whom he said, Fatimah is a part of me (Bukhari)
last: THE EYES WEEP, THE HEART GRIEVES.

lines: SHE WALKS EXACTLY LIKE HER FATHER.
cards: A young woman crosses a room in Medina, and the woman watching notices something: she walks exactly like her father. The watcher is Aisha, who tells this herself in Sahih al-Bukhari.
The father is the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, and he is ill. The daughter is Fatimah. He calls out, welcome, my daughter, and sits her beside him.
Then he leans close and whispers, and she starts to cry. He whispers again, and she laughs. Aisha asks what he said.
Fatimah won't tell her. Today: Fatimah, and the title she carries.

teach.h: FIRST WHISPER: HE WOULD NOT RECOVER.
teach.b: Fatimah kept the secret while her father lived. After he died, Aisha asked again, and this time she told; the reports in Bukhari give her answer. The first whisper: he would not recover from this illness.

teach.h: SECOND: SHE WOULD FOLLOW HIM SOON.
teach.b: The second, in one telling: she would be the first of his family to follow him; in another, she would be a leader among the women of paradise. So she laughed.
The news that comforted her was that she would not be apart from him for long.
That closeness runs through every report about them.
In the Sunan of Abu Dawud, Aisha says that when Fatimah came in, he would stand up for her, kiss her, and seat her in his own place; and when he came to her, she did the same for him.
A father standing up for his daughter. And in Bukhari he says it outright: Fatimah is a part of me, and whoever angers her angers me. Now the title.
In Arabic, al-Zahra means the radiant one, the shining one. The reports we just heard don't use it; later generations gave her the name, and explain it in different ways.
Sunni and Shi'a Muslims both use it and both honor her deeply. In Shi'a devotion her name is spoken in prayers and gatherings, and given to daughters.

teach.h: FATIMAH IS A PART OF ME.
teach.b: Across all of them, one picture holds: a daughter who walked like her father, sat in his seat, and was called a part of him.

how: Muslims speak of Fatimah with deep honor, often adding a blessing after her name; Shi'a Muslims in particular remember her in prayers and gatherings, and Muslim families name daughters after her.

o: the radiant one, a title Muslims give Fatimah
the eldest, a title for a prophet's first daughter
the weeping one, for her tears at his bedside

s: Fatimah told Aisha the secret right away
she kept it while her father lived, and told it only after he died.
when Fatimah came in, he would stand up for her
in Abu Dawud: he stood, kissed her, and seated her in his own place.
the deathbed reports call her al-Zahra
the title came later, and people explain it in different ways.

games.q: you're Fatimah. your father, ill, has just whispered something that made you cry and then laugh. Aisha asks what he said. what do you do?
o: keep his secret while he lives.
tell her only the happy part.
games.why: she kept the secret, and told it only after his death: he would not recover, and she would soon follow him.

practice: Bring to mind a daughter: yours, a niece, a student, a friend's girl, or yourself as someone's daughter, and in your mind stand up for her as she comes in, the way he stood for Fatimah, and give her your seat.
Hold one sentence of honor for her, plain and true. If you pray, make a quiet du'a for her; if not, just keep her in mind with care.

wordCard.voice: Al-Zahra. The radiant one: the title Muslims give Fatimah, the Prophet's daughter, whom he called a part of him. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the radiant, shining one; a title of Fatimah, daughter of the Prophet.

carryVoice: Your line: a part of him. Some love is said out loud, and stood up for. Day eight hundred eighteen, done.
